"Settings files and precedence - Claude Code Docs (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/configuration)
citeturn3view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"turn2search0","lineno":null}); Total lines: 400
L59: Claude Code reads settings from JSON settings files such as `~/.claude/settings.json`. It looks for them in a few locations, and cite10†the file it reads a setting from decides who the setting applies to . This page covers those files: which one to put a setting in, how to change a setting and confirm it applied, and which value Claude Code uses when the same key is set in more than one file.
L62: ##
L63: 
L64: cite10†​ L65: 
L66: Settings files and who they affect
L67: 
L68: Claude Code reads settings from four files, and an organization can also deliver managed settings from the claude.ai console. Each source has a scope: the set of people and projects a setting saved in it applies to, whether that’s just you, everyone in a project, or everyone in your organization.
L69: Scope  | File  | Who it affects  | Use it for
L70: --- | --- | --- | ---
L71: User  | `~/.claude/settings.json`  | You, in every project on this machine  | Personal preferences: theme, editor mode, default model, your own permission rules
L72: Shared project  | `.claude/settings.json`  | Everyone working in the folder that contains it. In a git repository, commit it so teammates get it  | Team permissions, hooks, plugins, and the environment variables the project needs
L73: Project local  | `.claude/settings.local.json`  | You, in this one project only. Claude Code keeps it out of git when it creates the file; if you create it by hand, add it to `.gitignore` yourself  | Personal overrides for one project, and testing before you share
L74: Managed  | `managed-settings.json` and other cite46†managed sources | Everyone your organization deploys it to; nothing you set overrides it, apart from a few cite37†security-sensitive exceptions | Security policy and compliance requirements
L75: In the File column, `~/.claude` is the `.claude` folder in your home directory, and a bare `.claude` is the `.claude` folder inside your project.
L76: ###
L77: 
L78: cite11†​ L79: 
L80: Compare the scope of each settings file
L81: 
L82: Suppose you have three projects on your machine, `website/`, `api/`, and `acme-app/`, a teammate has their own clone of `acme-app/`, and you start a cite38†cloud session on `acme-app/`. The graphic below shows which of those folders a setting applies in when you start Claude Code from them. Click a settings file to see the folders it reaches.
L83:   * `~/.claude/settings.json`: every project on your machine, and nothing on your teammate’s or in the cloud session
L84:   * `acme-app/.claude/settings.json`: your `acme-app/`. It reaches your teammate’s clone and the cloud session only if you commit the file to version control; until you do, it’s a file on your disk like any other and nobody else has it
L85:   * `acme-app/.claude/settings.local.json`: your `acme-app/` only. Claude Code adds it to your global git excludes the first time it writes the file, so it stays out of your commits; if you create the file by hand, cite14†add it to `.gitignore` yourself L86:   * Managed settings, whether a `managed-settings.json` file, an MDM policy, or cite47†server-managed settings from the claude.ai console: every project on every machine your organization deploys it to, or that you sign in to with your organization account. Only server-managed settings reach the cloud session
L87: ###
L88: 
L89: cite12†​ L90: 
L91: Find or create your settings files
L92: 
L93: Installing Claude Code doesn’t create any settings file. If your machine or project already has one, it came from one of these sources:
L94:   * Managed: your organization deploys it. You don’t create or edit it.
L95:   * Shared project: a project that already uses Claude Code may have one committed. If not, create it at `.claude/settings.json` in the project folder.
L96:   * User and Project local: create them yourself, or let Claude Code create them. It writes `~/.claude/settings.json` the first time you change an option in the `/config` menu that it stores in user settings, such as the theme, and `.claude/settings.local.json` the first time you give a standing approval on a permission prompt, such as “Yes, and don’t ask again” for a Bash command. A few `/config` options, including Show tips, save to `.claude/settings.local.json` instead of the user file.
L97: On Windows, `~/.claude` means `%USERPROFILE%\.claude`. To keep the home-directory files somewhere else, set cite48†`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` ; Claude Code then stores your settings, session history, and plugins there instead.
L98: 
L99: Claude Code also keeps a fifth file, cite49†`~/.claude.json` , that it writes for itself; you don’t need to edit it. It holds your sign-in session, cite50†MCP server configurations, per-project state such as trust decisions, and the cite51†global config keys that `/config` writes for you.
L100: ###
L101: 
L102: cite13†​ L103: 
L104: Share settings with your team
L105: Commit `.claude/settings.json` so everyone who clones the repository gets the same permissions, hooks, telemetry, and plugins. Each teammate can still override it for themselves in their own `.claude/settings.local.json`, so personal exceptions don’t need a commit. For a complete team file, see cite52†a team’s shared settings .
L106: Some of what you commit waits until each teammate cite53†trusts the folder , and a few keys never take effect from a repository file; cite54†Troubleshoot a setting that doesn’t apply covers both.
L107: ###
L108: 
L109: cite14†​ L110: 
L111: Keep personal settings out of a repository
L112: 
L113: To change a setting for yourself in one project without changing it for your teammates, save it in `.claude/settings.local.json` inside the project. Claude Code applies that file over the committed `.claude/settings.json`, so if your team’s file sets `"model": "claude-sonnet-5"` and you want Opus, put `"model": "claude-opus-4-8"` in your local file and only your sessions change. Three things to know about the local file:
L114:   * Claude Code writes it too. When Claude asks permission to run a Bash command and you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves that cite55†permission approval here as an `allow` rule.
L115:   * You don’t need to gitignore it yourself, unless you created it by hand. The first time Claude Code writes the file in a git repository that doesn’t already ignore it, it adds `**/.claude/settings.local.json` to your global git excludes file, so the file stays out of your commits in every repository.
L116: That file is `core.excludesFile` when your global git config sets it to an absolute or `~`-prefixed path; otherwise it’s `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore`, or `~/.config/git/ignore` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is unset. If you created the file by hand and Claude Code hasn’t written to it yet, add it to `.gitignore` yourself.
L117:   * Its allow rules don’t wait for trust while the file stays untracked. Because the file is yours and not the repository’s, Claude Code applies its `allow` rules without the cite53†workspace trust step it requires for the committed file. If the file is tracked by git, the trust step applies to it too; see cite56†When your local settings file needs trust .
L118: ####
L119: 
L120: cite15†​ L121: 
L122: Where Claude Code keeps the local file in a git repository
L123: When Claude asks permission to run a Bash command and you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves that approval as an `allow` rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`. If you start Claude Code in a subdirectory of a git repository, it reads and writes that file at the repository root and applies the approval across the whole repository. In a cite57†worktree , it uses the file at the main checkout’s root. Two rules qualify the root location:
L124:   * When the file stays with `.claude/settings.json` instead: outside a git repository, when the repository root is your home directory, on Windows, or when the repository root or its `.git` or `.claude` entry isn’t owned by your user.
L125:   * Paths in the file don’t anchor at the repository root: a permission rule that starts with `/` or a relative sandbox path cite58†anchors at the session’s primary working directory instead.
L126: Before v2.1.211, Claude Code kept the file in the starting directory. It still reads a file an earlier version left there alongside the root file; where both set the same key, the root’s value applies, and permission rules from both files apply. The Agent SDK’s cite59†`resolveSettings()` helper always reads the file from the starting directory.
L127: Claude Code reads the shared `.claude/settings.json` from the session’s cite60†primary working directory , so to use a file committed at the repository root, start Claude Code there. After you cite61†move the session with `/cd` , Claude Code reads both project files from the new directory instead, placing the local file by the same rules. Reading them from the directory you moved to requires Claude Code v2.1.246 or later.
L128: ###
L129: 
L130: cite16†​ L131: 
L132: Check what your organization enforces
L133: If your organization manages Claude Code, some settings are decided for you and nothing you put in your own files changes them. To see which, run `/status`: the `Setting sources` line names the managed source that applies to you. Managed settings apply wherever Claude Code runs on this machine; cite62†What a developer can change covers local admin rights and tools other than Claude Code. Managed settings reach you through the cite46†delivery mechanisms on the managed settings page, most commonly:
L134:   * cite47†Server-managed settings , which Claude Code fetches from the claude.ai admin console or a self-hosted cite63†Claude apps gateway L135:   * MDM or OS-level policies, and `managed-settings.json` files in a system directory
L136:   * An embedding host such as Claude Desktop, through the SDK `managedSettings` option; see cite64†Control policy from an embedding host L137: In a cite65†Cowork†claude.com session that runs on your machine in the Claude Desktop app, Claude Code doesn’t fetch server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console, and it reads policy deployed to your device unless your organization’s Claude Desktop configuration sets `requireCoworkFullVmSandbox`. cite66†Where and when a policy applies covers Cowork and cloud sessions.
L138: If you’re the administrator, cite4†Set up Claude Code for your organization walks through choosing what to enforce, and cite67†Deploy managed settings covers delivery and how to confirm a policy is in force.
L139: ##
L140: 
L141: cite17†​ L142: 
L143: Change a setting
L144: 
L145: You can change a setting from the `/config` menu, by editing a settings file, or for one session from the command line. Claude Code’s system prompt isn’t published. To give Claude standing instructions, use cite68†`CLAUDE.md` files or the `--append-system-prompt` flag.
L146: ###
L147: 
L148: cite69†​ L149: 
L150: Use the /config menu
L151: 
L152: Run `/config` inside Claude Code and open the Config tab. It lists a short set of personal options such as theme, editor mode, and verbose output, not every settings key. Select an option to change it; Claude Code saves it for you:
L153:   * Most options: `~/.claude/settings.json`
L154:   * A few options, such as Show tips: `.claude/settings.local.json`
L155:   * The cite51†global config options : `~/.claude.json`
L156: To set one option without the menu, pass `key=value`, such as `/config verbose=true`.
L157: 
L158: `/config` is part of the terminal interface. The cite42†VS Code chat panel and the cite44†desktop app don’t open it; change settings there by editing a settings file or through those apps’ own settings.
L159: ###
L160: 
L161: cite19†​ L162: 
L163: Edit a settings file
L164: 
L165: Open the settings file for the scope you want in your editor and add or change a key. Settings files are strict JSON: a `//` comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error, and Claude Code reports the file as a cite23†Settings Error at the next start. For example, to let Claude Code run your lint and test commands without asking and stop it reading `.env` files, add this to `~/.claude/settings.json`:
L166: ~/.claude/settings.json
L167: 
L168:     `{
L169:       "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
L170:       "permissions": {
L171:         "allow": [
L172:           "Bash(npm run lint)",
L173:           "Bash(npm run test *)"
L174:         ],
L175:         "deny": [
L176:           "Read(./.env)",
L177:           "Read(./.env.*)"
L178:         ]
L179:       }
L180:     }
L181:     `
L182: Each entry under `permissions` is a rule that names a tool and what it may do; cite41†Configure permissions explains the syntax. The `$schema` line points to the cite70†published JSON schema†json.schemastore.org for Claude Code settings, which gives you autocomplete and inline validation in VS Code, Cursor, and any other editor that supports JSON schema. The schema can lag behind the newest CLI releases, so a validation warning on a recently documented key doesn’t mean your configuration is invalid.
L183: After you save, run `/status` inside Claude Code to confirm the file loaded; cite71†Confirm what loaded says what the `Setting sources` line shows and how a broken file is reported. For a complete personal file, team file, and organization file, each shown with a comment on every key it sets, see the cite72†example settings files .
L184: ###
L185: 
L186: cite20†​ L187: 
L188: Change a setting for one session
L189: 
L190: To try a value without saving it, set it when you start Claude Code. The value applies to that session and your settings files stay as they were. You have three ways to do it:
L236: A managed `model` sets the model each session starts with, and you can still switch with `/model`; the lock is cite85†`availableModels` , which constrains `/model`, `--model`, and the `model` key in your own files. When your organization delivers more than one managed source, the rules for cite86†precedence within the managed tier say what Claude Code reads from each.
L237:   2. Command line arguments: flags you pass when you start `claude` from a terminal, for one session; see cite20†Change a setting for one session . Claude Code merges JSON you pass with `--settings <file-or-json>` with your settings files by the same rules as the other levels: it takes a key you set here over the same key in local, project, or user settings, and keeps the lower-level value for a key you omit.
L238:   3. Project local settings (`.claude/settings.local.json`): your personal settings for this project.
L239:   4. Shared project settings (`.claude/settings.json`): settings your team checks into source control.
L240:   5. User settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`): your personal settings for every project.
L241: Environment variables aren’t a level in this stack. When a behavior has both a shell variable and a settings key, which one applies is decided per pair, not by level: `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` exported in your shell applies over the `model` key from any file, while `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` applies only when no file sets `model`. The cite87†environment variables reference says which keys have a pair and which one Claude Code reads first.
L242: An `env` block inside a settings file is an ordinary key and follows the levels above. For a few security-sensitive keys, Claude Code honors a stricter value from a lower level over a managed value; cite37†Exceptions to managed settings precedence lists them.
L243: ###
L244: 
L245: cite25†​ L246: 
L247: Lists merge instead of overriding
L248: 
L249: When you set the same list key, such as `permissions.allow`, in more than one file, Claude Code combines the lists instead of picking one, so each file can add entries without removing another file’s. Four keys that hold model lists or per-model entries follow their own rules:
L250:   * cite88†`fallbackModel` is an ordered chain where position carries meaning, so Claude Code takes the whole value from the highest-precedence file that defines it.
L251:   * cite89†`modelPicker` holds one ordered list of rows plus a replace flag, so Claude Code never merges rows from two sources. It takes the whole value from the highest of managed settings, `--settings`, and user settings that defines it, and ignores the key in project and local settings. Requires Claude Code v2.1.242 or later.
L252:   * cite85†`availableModels` : when the managed settings Claude Code applies define it, Claude Code applies that list as-is and ignores entries you add in user, project, or local settings, unless an app that embeds Claude Code supplies its own model list; see cite37†Exceptions to managed settings precedence . Across managed sources the list never merges either; cite90†how Claude Code combines managed sources says which source’s list applies. Across non-managed scopes Claude Code merges the arrays as usual.
L253:   * cite80†`modelSettings` : Claude Code resolves it one model at a time, together with cite79†`effortLevel` . The `modelSettings` entry states which file’s value applies to a model.
L254: ###
L255: 
L256: cite26†​ L257: 
L258: Precedence examples
L259: 
L260: While Claude works, Claude Code shows a one-line tip under the spinner, such as “Use /config to change your default permission mode (including Plan Mode)”. Suppose you want those tips off, so you set cite91†`spinnerTipsEnabled` to `false` in `~/.claude/settings.json`. Each scenario below is something that can turn them back on, and what you can do about it.
L261: ####
L262: 
L263: cite27†​ L264: 
L265: Team settings override personal settings
L266: 
L267: Your team’s `.claude/settings.json` sets it to `true`. Claude Code uses the project value because shared project sits above user, so you see tips in that project and nowhere else. You can get your value back: add `"spinnerTipsEnabled": false` to `.claude/settings.local.json` in that project. Project local sits above shared project, so your sessions there stop showing tips and your teammates’ sessions don’t change.
L348: cite104†`remoteControlAtStartup` | `false` from `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`  | Honored even when a managed source sets `true`; a project or local `true` is ignored
L349: cite105†`crossSessionInbound` | A stricter value from `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`, on the `accept` < `hold` < `refuse` ladder  | Honored over managed, `--settings`, and user values; a project or local value that isn’t stricter is ignored
L350: cite106†`useAutoModeDuringPlan` | `false` from any managed source, `--settings`, `~/.claude/settings.json`, or `.claude/settings.local.json`  | Honored even when the winning managed source sets `true`; a `false` in `.claude/settings.json` is ignored
L351: cite107†`syncClaudeAiSkills` | `false` from any managed source, `--settings`, `~/.claude/settings.json`, or `.claude/settings.local.json`  | Honored even when the winning managed source sets `true`; a `false` in `.claude/settings.json` is ignored
L352: cite108†`maxEffortLevel` | A lower cap from any scope, including `--settings`  | Honored even when the managed settings Claude Code applies set a higher cap; the lowest cap applies. Requires Claude Code v2.1.267 or later
L353: An app that runs Claude Code inside itself and sets cite48†`CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST` is also an exception. Claude Code takes that app’s model configuration over the `model`, `fallbackModel`, `modelPicker`, and `modelOverrides` keys from every managed source, and over the model-selection variables in a managed `env` block, such as `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` and the `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` family. Claude Code keeps a managed cite85†`availableModels` allowlist in force unless the app supplies its own.
L354: ##
L355: 
L356: cite38†​ L357: 
L358: Settings in cloud sessions
L359: 
L360: A cloud session, on cite45†Claude Code on the web or from cite109†`claude --cloud` , runs in a cite110†cloud environment on a fresh clone of your repository, not on your machine. That changes which settings reach it:
L361:   * Shared project settings (`.claude/settings.json`): read, because the file is part of the clone. Commit a setting there to apply it in cloud sessions.
L362:   * User and project local settings (`~/.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`): not read. Both stay on your machine, and the local file isn’t in the clone.
L363:   * Managed settings: only cite47†server-managed settings reach a cloud session; a `managed-settings.json` file or MDM profile on your device doesn’t. A cite111†self-hosted environment also reads the managed settings file in its runner image. cite90†How Claude Code combines managed sources says when that file applies.
L364:   * `/config`: on the web, opens the Claude Code section of your claude.ai settings instead of changing a value. To change a setting for a cloud session, set an cite112†environment variable on the environment or commit the key to the repository’s `.claude/settings.json`.
L365: cite113†What carries over from your setup lists the rest: `CLAUDE.md`, skills, MCP servers, plugins, and credentials.
L366: ##
L367: 
L368: cite39†​ L369:

L88: 
L89: cite12†​ L90: 
L91: Find or create your settings files
L92: 
L93: Installing Claude Code doesn’t create any settings file. If your machine or project already has one, it came from one of these sources:
L94:   * Managed: your organization deploys it. You don’t create or edit it.
L95:   * Shared project: a project that already uses Claude Code may have one committed. If not, create it at `.claude/settings.json` in the project folder.
L96:   * User and Project local: create them yourself, or let Claude Code create them. It writes `~/.claude/settings.json` the first time you change an option in the `/config` menu that it stores in user settings, such as the theme, and `.claude/settings.local.json` the first time you give a standing approval on a permission prompt, such as “Yes, and don’t ask again” for a Bash command. A few `/config` options, including Show tips, save to `.claude/settings.local.json` instead of the user file.
L97: On Windows, `~/.claude` means `%USERPROFILE%\.claude`. To keep the home-directory files somewhere else, set cite48†`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` ; Claude Code then stores your settings, session history, and plugins there instead.
L98: 
L99: Claude Code also keeps a fifth file, cite49†`~/.claude.json` , that it writes for itself; you don’t need to edit it. It holds your sign-in session, cite50†MCP server configurations, per-project state such as trust decisions, and the cite51†global config keys that `/config` writes for you.
L100: ###
L101: 
L102: cite13†​ L103: 
L104: Share settings with your team
L105: Commit `.claude/settings.json` so everyone who clones the repository gets the same permissions, hooks, telemetry, and plugins. Each teammate can still override it for themselves in their own `.claude/settings.local.json`, so personal exceptions don’t need a commit. For a complete team file, see cite52†a team’s shared settings .
L106: Some of what you commit waits until each teammate cite53†trusts the folder , and a few keys never take effect from a repository file; cite54†Troubleshoot a setting that doesn’t apply covers both.
L107: ###
L108: 
L109: cite14†​ L110: 
L111: Keep personal settings out of a repository
L112: 
L113: To change a setting for yourself in one project without changing it for your teammates, save it in `.claude/settings.local.json` inside the project. Claude Code applies that file over the committed `.claude/settings.json`, so if your team’s file sets `"model": "claude-sonnet-5"` and you want Opus, put `"model": "claude-opus-4-8"` in your local file and only your sessions change. Three things to know about the local file:
L114:   * Claude Code writes it too. When Claude asks permission to run a Bash command and you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves that cite55†permission approval here as an `allow` rule.
L115:   * You don’t need to gitignore it yourself, unless you created it by hand. The first time Claude Code writes the file in a git repository that doesn’t already ignore it, it adds `**/.claude/settings.local.json` to your global git excludes file, so the file stays out of your commits in every repository.
L116: That file is `core.excludesFile` when your global git config sets it to an absolute or `~`-prefixed path; otherwise it’s `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore`, or `~/.config/git/ignore` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is unset. If you created the file by hand and Claude Code hasn’t written to it yet, add it to `.gitignore` yourself.
L117:   * Its allow rules don’t wait for trust while the file stays untracked. Because the file is yours and not the repository’s, Claude Code applies its `allow` rules without the cite53†workspace trust step it requires for the committed file. If the file is tracked by git, the trust step applies to it too; see cite56†When your local settings file needs trust .
L118: ####
L119: 
L120: cite15†​ L121: 
L122: Where Claude Code keeps the local file in a git repository
L123: When Claude asks permission to run a Bash command and you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves that approval as an `allow` rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`. If you start Claude Code in a subdirectory of a git repository, it reads and writes that file at the repository root and applies the approval across the whole repository. In a cite57†worktree , it uses the file at the main checkout’s root. Two rules qualify the root location:
L124:   * When the file stays with `.claude/settings.json` instead: outside a git repository, when the repository root is your home directory, on Windows, or when the repository root or its `.git` or `.claude` entry isn’t owned by your user.
L125:   * Paths in the file don’t anchor at the repository root: a permission rule that starts with `/` or a relative sandbox path cite58†anchors at the session’s primary working directory instead.
L126: Before v2.1.211, Claude Code kept the file in the starting directory. It still reads a file an earlier version left there alongside the root file; where both set the same key, the root’s value applies, and permission rules from both files apply. The Agent SDK’s cite59†`resolveSettings()` helper always reads the file from the starting directory.
L127: Claude Code reads the shared `.claude/settings.json` from the session’s cite60†primary working directory , so to use a file committed at the repository root, start Claude Code there. After you cite61†move the session with `/cd` , Claude Code reads both project files from the new directory instead, placing the local file by the same rules. Reading them from the directory you moved to requires Claude Code v2.1.246 or later.

content.text:
Found one actionable issue:

- `parseSiblingWorktrees` skips prunable entries but not Git’s `bare` records ([worktree_setup_diagnostic.go:84](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-metadata-followups/cmd/entire/cli/worktree_setup_diagnostic.go:84)). In this repository, `git worktree list --porcelain -z` includes `.bare` as a record, so it is treated as a sibling candidate. Usually this is harmless, but matching config files inside a bare common directory could create a false portability warning. Track a `bare` flag and exclude those records, with a parser regression.

Everything else audited cleanly:

- The sibling proof requires enabled project Entire settings, effective sibling enablement, and a recognizable shared Claude hook.
- Current disabled configurations and sibling local-only enablement remain silent.
- Current local-only Entire setup warns about portability without claiming capture is inactive.
- Claude user/local coverage is acknowledged. This agrees with current Claude Code scope semantics, including v2.1.211+ reading worktree-local settings from the main checkout.
- Doctor replaces the misleading Git-hooks `OK` only when the current worktree truly lacks both Entire settings scopes.
- JSON preserves `error: "not set up"` and adds only an optional `worktree_setup` object.
- Explicit sibling settings inspection does not replace the current worktree’s process-wide symlink-vouch policy.
- Malformed/unreadable configuration and ordinary unconfigured linked worktrees fail silently.

Focused CLI, settings, and Claude Code tests all passed.

Found one actionable issue:

- `parseSiblingWorktrees` skips prunable entries but not Git’s `bare` records ([worktree_setup_diagnostic.go:84](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-metadata-followups/cmd/entire/cli/worktree_setup_diagnostic.go:84)). In this repository, `git worktree list --porcelain -z` includes `.bare` as a record, so it is treated as a sibling candidate. Usually this is harmless, but matching config files inside a bare common directory could create a false portability warning. Track a `bare` flag and exclude those records, with a parser regression.

Everything else audited cleanly:

- The sibling proof requires enabled project Entire settings, effective sibling enablement, and a recognizable shared Claude hook.
- Current disabled configurations and sibling local-only enablement remain silent.
- Current local-only Entire setup warns about portability without claiming capture is inactive.
- Claude user/local coverage is acknowledged. This agrees with current Claude Code scope semantics, including v2.1.211+ reading worktree-local settings from the main checkout.
- Doctor replaces the misleading Git-hooks `OK` only when the current worktree truly lacks both Entire settings scopes.
- JSON preserves `error: "not set up"` and adds only an optional `worktree_setup` object.
- Explicit sibling settings inspection does not replace the current worktree’s process-wide symlink-vouch policy.
- Malformed/unreadable configuration and ordinary unconfigured linked worktrees fail silently.

Focused CLI, settings, and Claude Code tests all passed.
